summary: Survey report on implementations and deployments of PIM-SM, written as supporting documentation to advance the protocol from Proposed Standard to Internet Standard. It is an informational report rather than a protocol specification.

eli5.summary: A poll of who is using a multicast tool, to show it has been tried for real.

questions: what is a pim rendezvous point
why was the pim-sm survey done
subtitle: A survey of who implements and runs PIM-SM, gathered to support moving it to Internet Standard.

tldr.problem: To advance PIM-SM from Proposed Standard to Internet Standard, the IETF process requires evidence of interoperable implementations and real deployment.
tldr.mechanism: The PIM working group ran a questionnaire for operators and vendors that ended on 22 Oct 2012 and published the combined results.
tldr.outcome: PIM-SM was found widely implemented and deployed, but (*,*,RP) and PMBR had no deployments and one implementation, so they should be removed from the specification.

today: RFC 7063 is an Informational report and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is supporting evidence for advancing PIM-SM, not a protocol specification.

sections.title: Why a Survey Was Needed
sections.content:
PIM-SM was first published as RFC 2117 in 1997 and obsoleted by RFC 2362 in 1998, both Experimental. It was rewritten and advanced to Proposed Standard as RFC 4601 in 2006. The PIM working group decided to advance it to Internet Standard, and this survey is part of that work.

RFC 2026 requires at least two independent and interoperable implementations, and options not shown in at least two interoperable implementations must be removed. RFC 6410 cut the Standards Track to two maturity levels and asks for widespread deployment and no unused features that greatly increase implementation complexity.
sections.eli5: To graduate to the next grade, a tool must prove that several different people really use it. The survey collects that proof.

sections.title: How the Survey Worked and What Operators Said
sections.content:
A questionnaire was issued by the PIM working group co-chairs and announced widely to vendors and operators. It concluded on 22 Oct 2012. Responses stayed confidential and only combined results are published.

Nine operators responded. They reported PIM-SM use since 1998 in campus, enterprise, research and WAN networks, broadband ISPs and digital TV. Five deployments are based on RFC 4601 and two on RFC 2362, three operators run PIM-SM for IPv6, and six use equipment from multiple vendors. Only minor interoperability issues were reported and the vendors fixed them.

Except for one deployment alongside MOSPF, operators ran PIM-SM exclusively. No operator reported using (*,*,RP) or PMBR. RP counts ranged from a few (for example sixteen) to four hundred. Static configuration and Bootstrap Router (BSR) were both used for RP discovery, and Anycast-RP was used for redundancy. The best common practice seems to be static RP with Anycast-RP.
sections.eli5: Nine network owners answered. They have used the tool for years in schools, companies and TV, and it mostly just works.

sections.title: What Vendors Said
sections.content:
Eight vendors reported PIM-SM implementations: four based on RFC 4601, two on RFC 2362 and two hybrids. No vendor reported concerns about interoperability.

Most vendors have not implemented (*,*,RP) state or the PIM Multicast Border Router (PMBR), citing lack of deployment need, security concerns, or complexity and poor scalability. Only XORP reported implementing them, because they are part of the RFC 4601 specification.

Most vendors implement Source-Specific Multicast, join suppression, explicit tracking, the register mechanism, SPT switchover at the last-hop router, the assert mechanism and hashing of group to RP mappings. Some do not implement explicit tracking and SSM.
sections.eli5: The companies that build the equipment mostly built the same useful parts. Two odd parts were skipped by almost everyone.

sections.title: Key Findings and Security
sections.content:
The survey concludes that PIM-SM has been widely implemented and deployed and is well enough specified in RFC 4601 to give interoperable implementations. Because there are no deployments and only one known implementation of (*,*,RP) and PMBR, those features need to be removed from the specification as RFC 2026 and RFC 6410 require.

On security, the working group knows of at least three PIM-SM implementations that can use IPsec to protect PIM messages. In at least one, IPsec is configured separately using Security Policy Databases per RFC 5796. The appendix reproduces the operator and implementor questionnaires.
sections.eli5: The answer was that the tool works well, and the two unused parts should be dropped.
